answer: Yes. The private router (private.router, used for E2E tests) is only included when settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local". The ENVIRONMENT setting controls it. It defaults to local, and staging or production deployments don't mount it.

Operation IDs come from `custom_generate_unique_id` in backend/app/main.py. It is passed to FastAPI as `generate_unique_id_function`. Each ID is `{first tag}-{route function name}`, for example `users-read_users`. The frontend client is generated from these IDs. `operationId: true` in frontend/openapi-ts.config.ts is set for that generation.

Make sure the PR has exactly one of these labels: breaking, security, feature, bug, refactor, upgrade, docs, lang-all, internal. The label-checker `one_of` check in the check-labels job fails if the PR has none of them or has more than one. The labeler adds labels automatically, and you can add or remove them by hand. The check re-runs when you label or unlabel the PR.

Publishing a GitHub release (release event, type `published`) triggers the "Deploy to Production" workflow. It runs on a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner labeled `self-hosted` and `production`. The job is skipped in the main `fastapi` repository and only runs in user projects.
90% — the backend CI job runs `coverage report --fail-under=90`, so it fails if coverage is below 90%.

A pre-commit hook ("add-release-date") runs scripts/add_latest_release_date.py whenever release-notes.md is committed. The script finds the first header matching `## X.Y.Z`. If that header has no parenthesised date, it rewrites it as `## X.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)` using today's date from date.today().isoformat(). If the header already has a date, it leaves the file alone.

A pydantic model validator in the backend Settings (`_enforce_non_default_secrets`) checks SECRET_KEY, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD. If any of them is still "changethis", `_check_default_secret` raises a ValueError whenever ENVIRONMENT isn't "local", so the app fails at startup. In a local environment it only emits a warning.
8 days. The login endpoint builds the token with ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES, which is set to 60 * 24 * 8 minutes (11,520 minutes).
Up to 300 attempts (max_tries = 60 * 5, i.e. 5 minutes), retried with a fixed 1 second wait between attempts (wait_seconds = 1).

Startup fails. With ENVIRONMENT=staging and SECRET_KEY still "changethis", the Settings model validator (_enforce_non_default_secrets) calls _check_default_secret. That raises a ValueError: 'The value of SECRET_KEY is "changethis", for security, please change it, at least for deployments.' Only ENVIRONMENT=local gets a warning instead. The same check applies to POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD.

No. A superuser can't delete their own account through the users endpoints. DELETE /users/me returns 403 with "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves". The admin delete endpoint, DELETE /users/{user_id}, has the same guard. The tests in test_users.py check this for both endpoints.

The new endpoint's operationId will be `orders-<function_name>`. `custom_generate_unique_id` in `backend/app/main.py` returns `f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"`, and `route.name` defaults to the endpoint function's name. For example, a function named `read_orders` becomes `orders-read_orders`. The snippet doesn't show the `FastAPI(...)` call, so I'm assuming the function is passed there as `generate_unique_id_function`.

A superuser gets all items, with the count taken over every item. A normal user gets only the items they own (owner_id == current_user.id), and the count covers only those. Both are sorted by created_at descending (newest first), and both use skip/limit pagination (defaults 0 and 100). The response is ItemsPublic(data, count).

The backend CI job runs `uv run coverage report --fail-under=90` (in `.github/workflows/test-backend.yml`, line 40, working directory `backend`), so you need at least 90% coverage. Anything below 90% fails the job even when all tests pass.

The token is kept in the browser's localStorage under the key "access_token". `OpenAPI.TOKEN` reads it from there for each request. When a query or mutation fails with an ApiError whose status is 401 or 403, `handleApiError` removes "access_token" from localStorage and redirects the browser to /login (`window.location.href = "/login"`).

PrivateService comes from the private API routes, which exist only in local environments (they're for E2E tests). The generated client in src/client only includes PrivateService when it's generated against a local backend that exposes those routes. If the client is generated for another environment, the service is missing.

Run `bash ./scripts/generate-client.sh` from the top-level project directory, with the backend virtual environment activated, then commit the changes. The script does five things:
1. It `cd`s into `backend` and uses `uv run python` to import `app.main` and dump `app.openapi()` as JSON to `openapi.json`.
2. It moves `openapi.json` into `frontend/`.
3. It runs `bun run --filter frontend generate-client`, which runs `openapi-ts` (`@hey-api/openapi-ts`) and writes the TypeScript client from the schema.
4. It runs `bun run lint` to lint and format the result.
5. It stops on the first error (`set -e`).

The manual alternative is to download the OpenAPI JSON from `http://localhost/api/v1/openapi.json` into `frontend/openapi.json`, then run `bun run generate-client` in `frontend`.
8 days. ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 60 * 24 * 8 (11520 minutes). After the token expires, API calls return 401/403 and the frontend removes access_token and redirects to /login.

Yes. In corpus/frontend/playwright.config.ts, process.env.CI changes five settings. On CI, forbidOnly is true, so the build fails if test.only is left in. Retries are 2 locally 0. Workers is 1 (no parallel tests); locally it is undefined, so Playwright picks the default. The reporter is 'blob' (locally 'html'). reuseExistingServer is false for the webServer (`bun run dev`), so CI always starts a fresh server, while locally it reuses one that's already running.

Two UI guards keep regular users out of the admin page. First, the `/_layout/admin` route has a `beforeLoad` that calls `UsersService.readUserMe()`. If the user isn't a superuser, it throws a `redirect` to "/". Second, `AppSidebar` only adds the "Admin" link to its items when `currentUser?.is_superuser` is true, so regular users never see the link.

An admin (superuser) sees everybody's items: the backend's superuser branch counts and selects all `Item` rows with no owner filter. They come back ordered by `created_at` descending (newest first), with `skip`/`limit` pagination applied.
Backend: api.${DOMAIN}; Frontend: dashboard.${DOMAIN}; Adminer: adminer.${DOMAIN}

Give the runner the `production` label (it also gets the default `self-hosted` label), since the deploy job uses `runs-on: [self-hosted, production]`. The job is triggered by a GitHub `release` event of type `published`, i.e. when a release is published. It only runs in repos not owned by `fastapi`.
The backend service in compose.yml has a healthcheck that runs `curl -f http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check/`. It runs every 10s, times out after 5s, and allows 5 retries.

The prestart step waits up to about 5 minutes. In `backend_pre_start.py`, `max_tries = 60 * 5` (300 attempts) with `wait_seconds = 1` between tries, so it gives up after roughly 300 seconds. The snippet doesn't show the retry loop itself, but the values and the "5 minutes" comment point to that total.
The backend image runs `fastapi run --workers 4 app/main.py` by default. That starts the FastAPI app in production mode with 4 workers.
Reporter: 'blob' when CI is set (otherwise 'html'); retries: 2 (otherwise 0). The merge job then runs `playwright merge-reports --reporter html`.

The public Traefik gets its certificates from Let's Encrypt through an ACME certificate resolver named "le". It is configured with the EMAIL variable and uses the TLS challenge. The certificates are stored in /certificates/acme.json. That path is on the named Docker volume `traefik-public-certificates`, so they persist even if the container is recreated.
Run `docker compose watch`. The frontend is at http://localhost:5173 and the backend API is at http://localhost:8000. Swagger docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs.

The browser keeps the session token in localStorage under the key "access_token". The kick-out is the global handleApiError in main.tsx: any query or mutation that fails with an ApiError of status 401 or 403 removes access_token from localStorage and sets window.location.href to "/login". The token itself expires after ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES (8 days by default), which would also trigger a 401.

Open Mailcatcher's web interface at http://localhost:1080. With Docker Compose locally, the backend sends email over SMTP to the mailcatcher service (port 1025). Mailcatcher captures every message instead of sending it, so your password recovery email shows up there.
The link is valid for 48 hours (EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS = 48). It opens the frontend /reset-password page, with the token in the query string: {FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token=...

After deploying to production or staging, each service gets its own subdomain. Open `dashboard.example.com` for the web dashboard (the frontend) and `api.example.com` for the API (the backend). Replace `example.com` with your own domain.
docker compose exec backend bash scripts/tests-start.sh

The sidebar only adds the Admin item when currentUser.is_superuser is true (AppSidebar.tsx:23-25). Your account isn't a superuser, so the item isn't shown. If you go to /admin directly, the route's beforeLoad in admin.tsx (line 19) fetches the current user with UsersService.readUserMe(). We use Argon2 (via pwdlib) as the primary hasher. BcryptHasher stays in the PasswordHash list only so legacy hashes still verify. Old bcrypt accounts keep working. On a successful login, `verify_and_update` returns a new Argon2 hash. `authenticate` in crud.py then saves it to `db_user.hashed_password`, so the account is upgraded automatically.

Probably not through the main path. `authenticate` in `crud.py` runs `verify_password(password, DUMMY_HASH)` when the email isn't found, so the hashing cost, and therefore the response time, should be similar whether or not the email exists. The snippet is cut off, so I can't see the found-user branch or the login route that calls it. The release notes also say authentication was changed to take constant time to avoid enumeration attacks.

No. The forgot-password endpoint (POST /password-recovery/{email}) returns the same message whether or not the email has an account: "If that email is registered, we sent a password recovery link". It only sends the email when the user exists. This prevents email enumeration.
No. Sentry is only initialized when SENTRY_DSN is set and ENVIRONMENT is not "local". Developers running the backend locally use the "local" environment, so their errors aren't sent to Sentry.

A staging deployment is triggered by pushing or merging to the `master` branch (per `deployment.md`). It runs on a self-hosted runner labeled `staging` (`runs-on: [self-hosted, staging]`), and only in user projects, not when the repository owner is `fastapi`.

The `on:` trigger block of `deploy-staging.yml` isn't shown, so the branch trigger comes from the docs rather than the workflow file itself.

GitHub Actions updates are checked daily. The uv, bun, Docker (/backend and /frontend) and Docker Compose ecosystems are checked weekly. The only exclusion is the bun dependency "@hey-api/openapi-ts", which is ignored.

The `test-playwright` job in the Playwright Tests workflow splits the suite into 4 parallel shards. It uses a matrix with `shardIndex` set to [1,2,3,4] and `shardTotal` set to 4, and each shard runs `playwright test --shard=i/4` in docker compose. `fail-fast` is false. Each shard uploads a blob report, and a `merge-playwright-reports` job then merges them. The whole suite is skipped when the `changes` job (a dorny/paths-filter check) finds no changes in `backend/**`, `frontend/**`, `.env`, `compose*.yml` or `.github/workflows/playwright.yml`. In that case `changed` isn't 'true' and both the test and merge jobs don't run.

The backend lint script runs four checks on the `app` directory: mypy (type checking), ty check (type checking), ruff check (linting), and ruff format --check (formatting verification, with no changes written).

The API allows origins in settings.all_cors_origins: the configured BACKEND_CORS_ORIGINS list (comma-separated or list of URLs, default empty) plus FRONTEND_HOST. These are passed to CORSMiddleware as allow_origins, with credentials, all methods and all headers allowed.

The session token is NOT in an httpOnly cookie. The backend returns it in the JSON body of /login/access-token, and the frontend stores it in localStorage under "access_token" (useAuth.ts:45), so any JavaScript on the page can read it. No cookie is set anywhere; a search for set_cookie and httponly found nothing. It is wiped in two cases. First, on logout (useAuth.ts:56-57). Second, when any query or mutation gets an API 401 or 403 response (main.tsx:21-25). That handler removes the token and redirects to /login. Nothing else clears it. The JWT is valid for 8 days (ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 60*24*8, config.py), and the browser keeps the stored token until one of the cases above happens.

Production HTTPS certificates are issued automatically by Let's Encrypt through Traefik's "le" certificate resolver, which is configured with the `EMAIL` variable and stores its data in `/certificates/acme.json` (compose.traefik.yml). No, recreating the container doesn't lose them: `/certificates` is mounted from the named volume `traefik-public-certificates`, which persists across container recreation.

Deleting a user also permanently deletes that user's items. The admin delete dialog says "All items associated with this user will also be permanently deleted", and the backend route only calls `session.delete(user)` and commits. The cascade itself would have to be defined on the User/Item model relationship, which isn't in the code shown.

We use UUIDs, not auto-increment integers. The models define primary keys as `id: uuid.UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid.uuid4, primary_key=True)`. This applies to both the user model (line 50) and the item model (line 88). An Alembic migration, d98dd8ec85a3, converted the old integer IDs to UUIDs.
It raises an HTTPException with status 403 Forbidden and detail "Could not validate credentials" (when jwt.decode raises InvalidTokenError or the payload fails ValidationError).

On a successful login, authenticate() calls verify_password, which uses pwdlib's verify_and_update. For a legacy bcrypt hash this returns a new hash (Argon2, the first hasher in the PasswordHash). authenticate() then overwrites db_user.hashed_password with that new hash, commits it and refreshes the user. The row is silently upgraded from bcrypt to Argon2. If the password is wrong, nothing changes.

Settings falls back to the placeholder `"changethis"`. The README documents `secret_key` as defaulting to `"changethis"`, and `_check_default_secret` in `config.py` looks for that same value. When `ENVIRONMENT` is `"local"` it only emits a warning, and the code shown doesn't include the field definition itself.

The `emails_enabled` computed property in the settings decides it. It returns True only when both SMTP_HOST and EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL are set. `send_email` in utils.py asserts that this property is true before it sends anything.

Defaults (backend/app/core/config.py): SMTP_TLS=True, SMTP_SSL=False, SMTP_PORT=587, SMTP_HOST=None, SMTP_USER=None, SMTP_PASSWORD=None (also EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL/EMAILS_FROM_NAME=None). If both SMTP_TLS and SMTP_SSL are true, TLS wins: utils.py checks `if settings.SMTP_TLS` first and only uses `elif settings.SMTP_SSL` otherwise, so only tls=True is set.

Every password field in the request models has a minimum length of 8 and a maximum length of 128 characters. This covers UserCreate.password, UserRegister.password, UserUpdate.password (optional, but the same limits apply when it is set), UpdatePassword.current_password and new_password, and NewPassword.new_password. The line cited is UserCreate.password; the other fields are at lines 28, 35, 44, 45 and 129 of the same file.

PATCH /users/me/password can return: 400 "Incorrect password" (current_password doesn't match), 400 "New password cannot be the same as the current one" (new equals current), and 422 validation error for a bad request body. The auth dependency (CurrentUser) can also reject the request, e.g. 401/403 for a missing, invalid or inactive user.

It rejects the request with an HTTP 409 Conflict and the detail "User with this email already exists". The route looks up the user by the new email. If that user exists and is not the current user, it raises the error before any update is applied. Updating to your own current email is allowed.

A 403 Forbidden error with detail "Not enough permissions". This applies to GET, PUT and DELETE when the item exists and is owned by someone else, and the caller is not a superuser. If the item doesn't exist, the response is 404 "Item not found" instead.

Yes. POST /signup (register_user in users.py, mounted under the users router) creates a user without login. If the email already exists, it raises HTTPException 400 with detail "The user with this email already exists in the system". Otherwise it creates the user and returns UserPublic.

Run the `scripts/generate-client.sh` script (from the repo root). It dumps the backend's OpenAPI schema to `openapi.json`, moves it into `frontend/`, runs `bun run --filter frontend generate-client` to regenerate the TypeScript client, and then runs `bun run lint`.

The recovery email goes to the Mailcatcher container (schickling/mailcatcher) instead of a real mailbox. You can read it in the Mailcatcher web UI at http://localhost:1080. compose.override.yml sets these backend environment variables to route it there: SMTP_HOST="mailcatcher", SMTP_PORT="1025", SMTP_TLS="false" and EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL="noreply@example.com". Mailcatcher's SMTP port 1025 is also published to the host.

The backend tests use a session-scoped, autouse `db` fixture in `conftest.py`. It opens a Session and runs `init_db`, then yields the session to the tests. After all tests finish, it runs `delete(Item)` and `delete(User)` to remove every row from both tables, then commits.

The names come from each operationId, which the backend builds as "{tag}-{route name}" (custom_generate_unique_id in backend/app/main.py, e.g. "items-read_items"). In openapi-ts.config.ts the @hey-api/sdk plugin has asClass and operationId enabled. The class name is the tag, built with classNameBuilder "{{name}}Service" (ItemsService). The method name comes from methodNameBuilder. It takes the operation name, strips the service prefix if the name starts with it (ItemsReadItems becomes ReadItems), then lowercases the first letter. The result is readItems.

The /_layout route's beforeLoad calls isLoggedIn(). If that returns false, it redirects to /login. isLoggedIn() only checks that an "access_token" entry exists in localStorage. It does not check that the token is valid or unexpired. A bad or expired token is caught later: the API returns 401 or 403, and the global error handler in main.tsx removes the token and redirects to /login. The /_layout/admin route adds its own beforeLoad that calls readUserMe and requires is_superuser.

They're redirected to "/" (the home page). The /login route's beforeLoad checks isLoggedIn() and throws redirect({ to: "/" }). /signup does the same check (signup.tsx:45), as do recover-password and reset-password. isLoggedIn() only checks for an access token in localStorage.

In the frontend route definition for `/reset-password` (`reset-password.tsx`), the `beforeLoad` hook redirects to `/login` when `search.token` is missing. It also redirects to `/` first if the user is already logged in.

The email link is f"{settings.FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token={token}". FRONTEND_HOST defaults to http://localhost:5173, so by default the URL is http://localhost:5173/reset-password?token=<jwt>. The token is valid for EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS, which defaults to 48 hours. generate_password_reset_token uses that setting for the expiry.

A first-time visitor gets the "dark" theme, because main.tsx mounts ThemeProvider with defaultTheme="dark". ThemeProvider itself defaults to "system", but main.tsx overrides that. The provider reads localStorage first and falls back to the default only if nothing is stored. When the theme is changed, setTheme saves it to browser localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme".

The DataTable offers rows-per-page options of 5, 10, 25 and 50. The pagination controls, including the "Rows per page" select, appear only when `table.getPageCount() > 1`. If all rows fit on one page, they are hidden.

After creating an item (AddItem.tsx), only the "items" query is invalidated: invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["items"] }). After deleting an item (DeleteItem.tsx), invalidateQueries() runs with no key, so every cached query is invalidated and refetched. Both run in onSettled.

An ApiError is passed to handleError, which is bound to showErrorToast (`handleError.bind(showErrorToast)`). It calls extractErrorMessage. That function returns err.message for an AxiosError. Otherwise it reads err.body.detail. If detail is a non-empty array, it uses the first item's `.msg`. If not, it uses detail itself, or "Something went wrong." as a fallback. handleError then calls `this(errorMessage)`, which is showErrorToast. showErrorToast calls toast.error("Something went wrong!", { description }), so the extracted message becomes the toast description.

No. The code branches on `is_superuser`, but both branches give the same tabs. `tabsConfig` has only three tabs (My profile, Password, Danger zone). For superusers, `tabsConfig.slice(0, 3)` returns all three, and everyone else gets `tabsConfig` itself. The Playwright test also expects the same three tabs.

The API responds with HTTP 403 and the detail "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves", so nothing is deleted. In the frontend, the global `MutationCache` `onError` handler in `main.tsx` treats any 401 or 403 `ApiError` the same way: it removes `access_token` from localStorage and redirects to `/login`. The `DeleteAccount` component isn't shown, so I'm assuming its delete call goes through that mutation cache and doesn't add its own error handling.

No. The profile form (UserInformation.tsx) limits full_name to 30 characters with z.string().max(30). The API limits it to 255 (max_length=255 in the backend models, and maxLength: 255 in the generated schemas).

The actions column renders `<UserActionsMenu user={row.original} />` for every row (columns.tsx:69). However, `UserActionsMenu` returns `null` when `user.id === currentUser?.id` (UserActionsMenu.tsx:23), so your own row shows no menu. This prevents you from editing or deleting your own account from the admin table.

The prestart service runs `bash scripts/prestart.sh` (set in compose.yml). That script does three things in order:
1. `python app/backend_pre_start.py`, which waits for the DB to be ready.
2. `alembic upgrade head`, which runs the migrations.
3. `python app/initial_data.py`, which creates the initial data in the DB.

The backend service waits for prestart to finish with `service_completed_successfully`.

The `db` service in `compose.yml` runs the `postgres:18` image. Its health check runs `pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d ${POSTGRES_DB}` every 10s (10s timeout, 5 retries, 30s start period). Data is stored in the named volume `app-db-data`, mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata`, which is also the `PGDATA` path.
The backend reports to Sentry in every environment except "local", provided SENTRY_DSN is set. In practice that means staging and production, and any other non-local ENVIRONMENT value.

compose.yml (production) bakes in VITE_API_URL=https://api.${DOMAIN}. compose.override.yml (local development) bakes in VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8000. The playwright service in the override file uses http://backend:8000, but that is a separate image from the frontend.

Deep links: nginx.conf serves static files from /usr/share/nginx/html with `try_files $uri /index.html =404`. Any path that isn't a real file falls back to /index.html, so the SPA router handles it. The same file includes /etc/nginx/extra-conf.d/*.conf. The Dockerfile copies nginx-backend-not-found.conf into that directory, and it returns 404 for /api, /docs and /redoc. Those paths are not served by the frontend.

The dashboard is exposed through Traefik's internal service `api@internal`, on an HTTPS router for host `traefik.${DOMAIN}`. That router uses TLS with a Let's Encrypt certificate from the `le` resolver. It is protected by the `admin-auth` HTTP Basic Auth middleware, which takes its credentials from the `USERNAME` and `HASHED_PASSWORD` environment variables. The HTTP router for the same host only redirects to HTTPS, using the `https-redirect` middleware.
The `traefik-public` Docker network must exist on the remote server. Create it by running `docker network create traefik-public` on the server.

The staging runner needs the label `staging`. It also has to be a self-hosted runner, so it carries the `self-hosted` label that GitHub adds automatically. The "Deploy to Staging" workflow uses `runs-on: [self-hosted, staging]`. It runs on every push to `master`, but only when the repository owner isn't `fastapi`. When the runner setup asks about labels, enter `staging`. You can also add the label later.

No. The unauthenticated create-user endpoint (POST /api/v1/private/users/) lives in the private router, which is only mounted when settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local". Production deploys set ENVIRONMENT=production, so it is not reachable there. (Note: the public self-registration endpoint /api/v1/users/signup is always mounted.)

For the backend service, `docker compose watch` syncs the `./backend` directory into `/app/backend` in the container. It ignores `./backend/.venv` and `.venv`. It rebuilds the service when `./backend/pyproject.toml` changes.

The local stack (compose.override.yml) publishes these host ports: 80 and 8090 (proxy; 8090 maps to container port 8080), 5432 (db), 8080 (adminer), 8000 (backend), 1080 and 1025 (mailcatcher), 5173 (frontend, mapped to container port 80) and 9323 (Playwright report). compose.traefik.yml separately publishes 80 and 443, but that file is not part of the local override.

It's a smoke test that the stack builds and starts. On pushes to master and on PRs (opened/synchronize), it runs `docker compose build`, then `down -v --remove-orphans`, then `up -d --wait backend frontend adminer`. `--wait` makes it wait for those services to be running or healthy. It then curls the backend health check (http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check) and the frontend (http://localhost:5173). Last, it tears everything down with `down -v --remove-orphans`. It runs no unit tests. It only checks that the images build, the services start, and the backend and frontend respond.

In the Test Backend workflow, only the `db` and `mailcatcher` services run in containers. They are started with `docker compose up -d db mailcatcher`. Everything else runs directly on the ubuntu-latest runner: checkout, Python and uv setup, the DB migration (`uv run bash scripts/prestart.sh`), the tests (`uv run bash scripts/tests-start.sh`), the coverage artifact upload and `uv run coverage report`. The backend app itself is not run in a container. The `docker compose down -v --remove-orphans` steps tear the containers down before and after the tests.

Yes. Stop the backend container with `docker compose stop backend`. Then run `cd backend` and `fastapi dev app/main.py` to start the local backend with auto-reload. The Docker and local services use the same ports, so the rest of the stack keeps working without config changes.
Yes. The Traefik UI shows how the proxy is handling routes. In local development it's at http://localhost:8090. The local proxy service maps host port 8090 to Traefik's internal port 8080.

Set `DOMAIN=localhost.tiangolo.com` in your `.env` and run with Docker Compose. The local Traefik proxy in `compose.override.yml` (port 80) will then serve the backend at `http://api.localhost.tiangolo.com` and the frontend at `http://dashboard.localhost.tiangolo.com`, while the plain ports (8000 and 5173) still work.

Install the prek git hook in your local repo. From the `backend` folder, run `uv run prek install -f`. This writes the hook to `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, so the checks run automatically before each commit. The `-f` flag overwrites any pre-commit hook that's already there. prek is already a project dependency, and the config is in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` at the project root.

Inside the backend container (`docker compose exec backend bash`), run `alembic revision --autogenerate -m "Describe your change"` to create the migration. Commit the generated files. Then apply it with `alembic upgrade head`.

Yes. The tests write the HTML coverage report to `htmlcov/index.html`. In the container that is `/app/backend/htmlcov`. `compose.override.yml` bind-mounts `./backend/htmlcov` on the host to `/app/backend/htmlcov` in the backend service. The label check (`agilepathway/label-checker` in `.github/workflows/labeler.yml`) requires the PR to have exactly one of these labels: `breaking`, `security`, `feature`, `bug`, `refactor`, `upgrade`, `docs`, `lang-all`, or `internal`. The code doesn't say which fits your PR, so ask the maintainer for whichever matches your change, such as `bug` for a fix or `docs` for a documentation change.

The `prestart` service in compose.yml runs `bash scripts/prestart.sh`. That script waits for the DB, runs `alembic upgrade head` to create the tables, then runs `python app/initial_data.py`. `initial_data.py` calls `init_db`, which creates the first superuser.

Open the theme (appearance) toggle/dropdown in the dashboard and choose "Light" (the light-mode item calls setTheme("light")). Yes, it is remembered: setTheme saves the choice to the browser's localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme" and it is read back on load. The default is dark if nothing has been saved. The choice is per browser, not per account.
